bull_thesis: CIE Automotive is a Spanish maker of metal and plastic car parts that has done something almost none of its competitors have managed: it keeps growing and keeps earning good margins while the global car market shrinks. On 23-24 July 2026 it reported the best half-year in its history - sales of EUR 2,103.8m (up 5.2%), operating cash profit (EBITDA, earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation) of EUR 401.1m at a 19.1% margin, the first time it has passed EUR 400m in a half, operating profit of EUR 300.5m at 14.3%, and net profit of EUR 191.3m. It turned 71.2% of that cash profit into operating cash flow against its own 65% target, and it did so while paying EUR 70.3m to shareholders and EUR 172.7m for acquisitions, yet still cut borrowings to 1.19 times cash profit from 1.26 times a year earlier. Strip out the currency translation and the business grew 9.3% against a world market that shrank 1.0%; strip out the acquisition too and organic growth was still about 5%, roughly six points better than the market. The shares change hands at EUR 25.85, which is about 8.6 times what the company should earn this year and a free-cash-flow yield above 10%. The parts are worth more than the whole. CIE owns 65.7% of a separately listed Indian subsidiary, CIE Automotive India, quoted in Mumbai at about EUR 1.44bn, so that stake alone is worth roughly EUR 944m - 31% of the parent's entire EUR 3.07bn market value - for a business that is only 16.8% of sales. The Indian arm trades at about 17.5 times earnings while the parent trades at 8.6 times. Value the four other regions on their own operating cash profit at multiples the market actually pays for auto suppliers, add the Indian stake at its quoted price, subtract the EUR 962m of net borrowings, and the parts sum to roughly EUR 30 on this year's earnings power and EUR 33.50 on next year's. Ten analysts covering the stock carry targets of roughly EUR 33.60 to EUR 39.50. There is a dated, escalating cash-return commitment behind it: the dividend payout rises to 42% of profit for 2026 and 50% for 2027, which at today's price is a yield heading toward 6%, with borrowings guided below 0.7 times cash profit by the end of 2027. The acquisition record supports the model - Aludec, bought for about EUR 200m of enterprise value and completed on 3 March 2026, was contributing EUR 17.3m of operating profit within four months. Over ten years the company has compounded sales at 6% and cash profit at 8% and lifted its operating margin from 11.4% to 14.3%, through a pandemic, a chip famine and an energy shock. The conditions the case depends on: European and Brazilian share gains must continue at roughly the current pace; the Indian subsidiary must hold its Mumbai valuation; the North American business must stop shrinking once the tariff regime settles; and the cash earmarked for acquisitions must be spent as well as it was on Aludec.
bear_thesis: The record headline is largely bought, not earned. Aludec contributed EUR 13.5m of the first half's EUR 191.3m of net profit and EUR 82.7m of the roughly EUR 104m of sales growth. Take the acquisition out and CIE's first-half profit fell about 4.4% year on year, from EUR 185.9m to roughly EUR 177.8m, and organic reported sales grew about 1%. The much-quoted 10.3 points of market outperformance is about 6 points once the acquisition is removed from the constant-currency figure. Meanwhile the gap between operating profit and net profit is widening - cash profit grew 5.8% and operating profit about 5.1% but net profit only 2.9% - because interest on the money spent buying Aludec and the share of earnings owed to minority shareholders in India are both rising. The end market is contracting: global light-vehicle production is forecast at 91.1 million units in 2026 against 93.1 million in 2025, with the second half expected down about 3%. Two of the five regions are already going backwards and losing share - North America, 25.7% of sales, fell 3.4% against a market down about 1%, and China fell 11.7%, underperforming by more than six points as local carmakers bring work in-house. North America also sits directly in an unresolved tariff regime: the United States' Section 122 authority lapsed by statute on 24 July 2026, the same week CIE reported, and the proposed replacement covering roughly 60 economies at 10% to 12.5% is not final. Management described shifting production from Mexico to the United States but quantified neither the cost nor the capital required. Margins are the other problem. The 19.1% cash-profit margin is an all-time high, about 1.26 standard deviations above the company's own historical peak, and it is flat year on year rather than still expanding - so the low multiple is a low multiple on peak profitability in a shrinking market, which is exactly the setup where cheapness proves illusory. Return on invested capital of 9.4%, while improving, is only around the cost of capital for a leveraged cyclical, and the balance sheet carries EUR 1.76bn of goodwill against EUR 1.45bn of equity attributable to shareholders - growth has been bought repeatedly and there is almost no tangible book value underneath it. Then there is the capital-allocation problem, which is the sharpest item in the file. On the 24 July call the board said it is very unhappy with the share price and, in the same breath, ruled out buying back stock at current levels while several acquisition targets enter due diligence in August and September, with management flagging a possible significant leap in scale. A board that will not buy its own shares at 8.6 times earnings and a 10% cash yield is telling shareholders it prefers other people's assets - which removes the one lever that would mechanically close the discount and replaces it with deal risk, at the top of the balance sheet, into a falling market. Management itself said the published consensus for net profit is somewhat optimistic. Raw-material costs for plastics and aluminium are rising with Brent crude near USD 89 and the Strait of Hormuz blockaded again since mid-July 2026. The stock trades within about 3% of its 52-week low of EUR 25.05 the week after record results, roughly 10% below its 200-day average, on about EUR 2m of daily turnover - the market has seen these numbers and declined to pay up, and analysts' targets have been cut repeatedly on the way down. What would confirm the bear case: a large debt-funded acquisition announced in the autumn window; a second-half operating margin below 18.5%; another quarter of North American and Chinese share loss; or a de-rating in the Indian subsidiary, which is already 21% below its own 52-week high.
consensus_delta: For a deep-value name the question is whether the market is pricing terminal decline into a company with stable or growing earnings power. Here the answer is: partly, and the market is more right than the bulls admit - but it is wrong on two specific, checkable points. Where the street is wrong. First, on the Indian subsidiary. The published research treats CIE as a single European auto supplier and applies a single European auto-supplier multiple to the whole company. But 65.7% of CIE Automotive India is quoted in Mumbai at about EUR 944m, which is 31% of the parent's entire EUR 3.07bn market value, and that market is paying about 17.5 times earnings for the same assets the European market is refusing to pay 9 times for. Nothing in the analyst commentary I could find marks that stake to its own price. Value the Indian holding at its quoted price and the rest of CIE - Europe, North America, Brazil, China, roughly EUR 284m of attributable earnings - is being valued at about EUR 2.1bn, or seven and a half times. That is the specific mispricing. Second, on currency. Reported sales grew 5.2% while constant-currency sales grew 9.3%; the 4.1-point gap is Indian rupee and Brazilian real weakness against the euro, and the consensus has extrapolated that headwind. The euro has since weakened against the dollar (1.1377 against a 200-day average near 1.16), which would turn part of that drag into a tailwind in the second half - a translation swing the models are not carrying. Where the street is wrong in the other direction, and this is the part a bull must own. The consensus for 2026 earnings of about EUR 3.09 a share is too high, and I know that because management said so on the 24 July call, describing the Bloomberg consensus for net results as somewhat optimistic. My own build - second-half profit similar to the first half adjusted for the usual seasonal step-down, plus a full contribution from Aludec - lands at EUR 2.90 to EUR 3.05. The published price targets of roughly EUR 33.60 to EUR 39.50 from ten analysts have been serially cut as the shares fell from a EUR 33.00 high to EUR 25.85, and a target range 30% to 50% above a stock sitting at its 52-week low is a signal that the sell side is behind the tape, not ahead of it. So the genuine disagreement is narrower than the headline gap: the market is right that earnings growth has stalled (up 2.9%, and down about 4% excluding the acquisition) and right that the end market is shrinking; it is wrong to value the Indian stake at nothing distinctive and wrong to treat a 19% cash-profit margin business as though it were Forvia.
forcing_function: There is no hard, dated event that forces a re-rating, and that is the central honest weakness of this case. The nearest thing to a forcing function is the acquisition decision running through August and September 2026, and it is two-sided rather than asymmetric: management said several targets are in due diligence and that a completed transaction could produce a significant leap in scale. If a deal is announced at Aludec-like economics - roughly EUR 200m of enterprise value for a business annualising well into double-digit millions of operating profit - it validates the capital-allocation model and gives the market a concrete reason to re-price. If it is large and debt-funded, it does the opposite. The second candidate is the 2027 dividend step to a 50% payout, which at today's price implies a yield near 6% alongside net borrowings guided below 0.7 times cash profit; that is a company policy on a stated year rather than a binding commitment, and it works slowly. The third and cleanest potential trigger has been explicitly refused: a buyback. On the 24 July 2026 call the board said it was very unhappy with the share price and ruled out repurchases at current levels. A board that reverses that decision - authorising a buyback at 8.6 times earnings and a 10%-plus free-cash-flow yield - would be the single most powerful re-rating event available to this company, and it is the specific development to watch for. The fourth is structural and unscheduled: the holding-company discount around the 65.7% stake in CIE Automotive India, worth about EUR 944m at market against a EUR 3.07bn parent. A partial sell-down, a demerger, or an activist pressing on that gap would crystallise it - but management stated on the same call that no portfolio share sales are planned, so nothing is in motion. Scheduled dates from here: third-quarter trading statement expected late October 2026; full-year 2026 results expected late February 2027, which is also when the 2027 payout step becomes concrete.
valley_of_death: The next three to nine months carry four specific hazards, and none of them is a cash-burn or refinancing problem - the balance sheet is the strong part of this story. First and largest, the acquisition window. Management said on 24 July 2026 that several targets enter due diligence in August and September and flagged a possible significant leap in scale. Any announcement lands in exactly this window. A deal bought at Aludec-like economics is a positive; a large, debt-funded one on a shrinking market would push net borrowings back above 1.5 times cash profit, break the stated path to below 0.7 times by end-2027, and very likely take the shares through the EUR 25.05 low. This is the dominant near-term risk and it is entirely management's choice. Second, the second-half production step-down. The company itself guides to global light-vehicle production falling about 3% in the second half, and expects its own second half to look like the first apart from seasonality - which means an absolute decline. Third-quarter numbers, due late October 2026, are the first test, and against a stock that just failed to re-rate on record numbers, an in-line-but-declining print is not obviously enough. Third, tariffs and raw materials, both live and both unresolved. The United States' Section 122 authority lapsed by statute on 24 July 2026 and the proposed replacement covering roughly 60 economies at 10% to 12.5% is not final; North America is 25.7% of CIE's sales, is already shrinking 3.4%, and management has not quantified the cost of the Mexico-to-United-States reallocation it described. Separately, with Brent crude near USD 89 and the Strait of Hormuz blockaded again since mid-July 2026, plastic and aluminium input costs are rising, and CIE passes those through with a lag - a one-to-two-quarter margin squeeze before recovery, which is precisely the window where a 19.1% margin at 1.26 standard deviations above its own historical peak has the most to lose. Fourth, the Indian leg. CIE Automotive India is 21% below its own 52-week high and trades at about 17.5 times earnings; a de-rating of the Indian mid-cap tape would cut roughly EUR 2 a share off the sum-of-the-parts without anything happening in the operating business. There is no debt maturity wall - liquidity was EUR 1,658.8m at 30 June 2026 (EUR 757.2m of cash plus EUR 711.9m of undrawn facilities) against net financial debt of EUR 962.4m - and no dividend risk at a 42% payout covered roughly two and a half times by free cash flow.
positioning_washout: There is no mechanical forced-selling event on the horizon, and that is a limitation of the setup rather than a comfort. The dividend is rising, not being cut, so income holders have no trigger to liquidate; the payout goes to 42% for 2026 and 50% for 2027, which at EUR 25.85 is a yield climbing from roughly 4.7% toward 6%. The company is not in a major global index whose reconstitution would force flows, and no spin-off, distribution or corporate action is scheduled. What is present is a slow, discretionary washout rather than a mechanical one. The shares have fallen from a 52-week high of EUR 33.00 to EUR 25.85, are about 10% below the 200-day average of EUR 28.60 and 6% below the 50-day of EUR 27.59, and now sit within about 3% of the 52-week low of EUR 25.05 - a persistent, unpanicked bleed, the pattern of index-agnostic European small and mid-cap money reducing auto exposure at its own pace. The screening data corroborates a thin ownership base: a smart-money score of 12 out of 100 and neutral institutional flow. Liquidity is the practical constraint - about 80,000 shares changed hands on 27 July 2026, roughly EUR 2m of value, so any position must be sized to be exitable over days, not hours, and a genuine flush would be violent in a stock this thin. The absence of a forced seller cuts both ways: it means no artificially depressed entry is being handed to us, and it means nothing mechanical will lift the price either. Note one asymmetry: the board has said it is unhappy with the valuation but will not buy back stock, so there is no company bid underneath the shares to absorb selling - unusual, and a genuine negative for anyone waiting for the price to be defended.
moderator_conclusion: This is a good business at a fair-to-good price with nothing to make the market notice, and the right call is to wait for a better entry with a named trigger rather than to buy it here. Start with what is genuinely strong. CIE Automotive is the quality name in a wrecked sector: a 19.1% operating cash margin and 14.3% operating margin against European peers running high-single digits and losing money, a decade of 6% sales and 8% cash-profit compounding through a pandemic and a chip famine, cash conversion of 71.2% against its own 65% target, and borrowings falling to 1.19 times cash profit even while it bought a company and raised the dividend. The forensic file is clean and management is candid to the point of telling the market its consensus is too high. At EUR 25.85 the shares are about 8.6 times this year's likely earnings with a free-cash-flow yield above 10%, and inside that price sits a 65.7% stake in a Mumbai-listed subsidiary worth about EUR 944m, or 31% of the whole company's market value - a measurable holding-company discount that nobody covering the stock appears to be marking. Now the reasons that is not enough to buy today. The record half is largely bought: excluding Aludec, first-half profit fell about 4.4% year on year, and 80% of the sales growth came from the acquisition. The margin is at an all-time high, roughly 1.26 standard deviations above its own historical peak, and flat rather than still rising - so the cheap multiple is a cheap multiple on peak profitability in an end market forecast to shrink from 93.1 to 91.1 million vehicles. Two of five regions are shrinking and losing share, and one of them, North America at 25.7% of sales, sits inside a tariff regime that changed by statute in the same week the company reported and has not settled. And the board, having called its own shares undervalued, declined to buy them and pointed the cash at acquisitions entering due diligence in August and September - which hands the outcome to a deal nobody can see yet and removes the one mechanism that would close the discount without the market's cooperation. Applying the current regime read: this thesis does not lean on rate cuts, which is a genuine plus with a hawkish Federal Reserve and a December hike still the base case, and its resolution driver - global light-vehicle production and European industrial demand - is largely independent of the two factors now swamping the book, artificial-intelligence capital spending and oil, apart from a real raw-material channel with Brent near USD 89. That independence is worth something for portfolio construction. But there is no live dated driver to reward, so the regime tilt moves nothing here in either direction, and the fired first-half print is neither credit nor penalty in this lane - the residual value case has to stand on its own, and it stands at about 22% upside to a EUR 31.50 base against about 16% downside to EUR 21.75, with the 52-week low only 3% away. That is a real but ordinary reward for a thin, cyclical, acquisition-hungry mid-cap. So: wait, with two specific triggers. Buy on a break of the EUR 25.05 52-week low that carries the shares into the EUR 22 to EUR 23 zone - which the second-half production decline, a tariff cost, or a poorly received acquisition could easily produce - because at EUR 22.50 the same parts arithmetic turns an ordinary setup into a compelling one. Or buy at this price on the day the board reverses itself and authorises a buyback, which would confirm that management values its own equity the way its own numbers say it should. Absent either, the value case is sound and the timing is not. Separately, on the value question alone - ignoring the missing catalyst and the regime entirely - this is a four: a demonstrably well-run, cash-generative franchise with a clean forensic record trading meaningfully below what its parts are worth. What holds it back from a five is not the business and not the balance sheet, but the suspicion that a record margin in a shrinking market is the numerator that makes the multiple look low.
sop_breakdown: Base case is a geographic sum-of-the-parts using the regional split of operating cash profit (EBITDA) the company disclosed for the first half of 2026, with the separately listed Indian subsidiary marked at its own Mumbai share price instead of a multiple, because that is a hard, observable number rather than an assumption. On this year's expected cash profit of about EUR 795m the parts are: Europe (39.0%, EUR 310m) at 5.5 times enterprise value to cash profit = EUR 1,705m; North America (26.4%, EUR 210m) at 6.0 times = EUR 1,260m; Brazil (13.0%, EUR 103m) at 5.5 times = EUR 567m; China (5.7%, EUR 45m) at 3.5 times = EUR 158m. Those four sum to EUR 3,690m. Add the 65.7% holding in CIE Automotive India, worth EUR 944m at its quoted price (INR 15,677 crore at 109.09 rupees to the euro), less a 10% holding-company discount for the fact that a controlling stake in a listed subsidiary is not freely realisable, giving EUR 850m. Subtract net financial debt of EUR 962.4m as the company reported it on 30 June 2026, and about EUR 40m for non-Indian minority interests. That gives EUR 3,538m of equity, or EUR 29.83 a share on 118.6m shares. Running the same exercise on next year's consensus cash profit of EUR 863m with net debt at EUR 850m gives EUR 33.46. I take EUR 31.50 as the base, between the two, because the 18-month horizon straddles both years. Note on the debt definition: EUR 962.4m is the company's own net financial debt measure at 30 June 2026. Adding the EUR 73m of capitalised leases on the balance sheet would take it to roughly EUR 1.04bn and cut the base value by about EUR 0.65 a share. Cross-checks on EUR 31.50: 10.5 times this year's likely earnings of about EUR 3.00 a share, 9.5 times next year's consensus EUR 3.31, and a free-cash-flow yield of about 8.7% on roughly EUR 325m of free cash flow - all reasonable for a business compounding cash profit at 8% a decade with leverage at 1.19 times. It also sits about 6% below the low end of the published analyst target range of EUR 33.60 to EUR 39.50, which is the appropriately skeptical posture given how often those targets have been cut on the way down.
risk_reward: Levels, not ratios. The shares trade at EUR 25.85. My base-case fair value is EUR 31.50 and my adverse case is EUR 21.75, so the distance up to fair value is somewhat larger than the distance down to the adverse case, but not dramatically so - this is not a two-for-one setup at today's price. The adverse case sits about 13% below the current 52-week low of EUR 25.05, which is only about 3% under the market price, so there is very little technical cushion between here and a fresh low. There is no structural floor: the company carries net debt of roughly EUR 962m rather than net cash, there is no tender or deal price, and the listed Indian stake, while worth about EUR 944m, is a controlling holding the board has explicitly said it will not sell. The dividend, heading toward a 50% payout in 2027, is income, not a floor. Note also that the acquisition pipeline entering due diligence in August and September is a two-sided risk to these levels: a good deal at Aludec-like economics lifts the base case, a large debt-funded one lowers the adverse case.
peer_comps_note: The supplied peer file calls CIE cheap versus its peers on net margin and price-to-free-cash-flow. That verdict needs correcting against live multiples, and the correction cuts both ways. Measured on enterprise value to operating cash profit (EBITDA) as of 27 July 2026, the group trades at: Forvia 3.46 times, Valeo 3.56 times, Denso 5.06 times, Magna 7.25 times, Continental 9.96 times. CIE, at a market value of EUR 3.07bn plus EUR 962m of net debt plus the roughly EUR 493m market value of the Indian minority, on trailing cash profit of about EUR 768m, trades at roughly 5.8 times. So CIE is not cheap against the two distressed European names - it is at a premium to them, and it deserves to be, because it earns a 19.1% cash-profit margin against their high-single to low-double digits and a 23% return on equity against Forvia's negative and Valeo's 6%. It is roughly in line with Denso and clearly below Magna, whose 7.25 times is paid for a business with an operating margin around a third of CIE's. On enterprise value to sales, at about 1.1 times, CIE is the most expensive in the group apart from Continental - again, because the margins are far better. The honest conclusion: CIE is cheap relative to its own quality and to its own history, not cheap relative to a peer group that is itself in the bargain bin. And the discount is substantially shared-factor, not name-specific - every one of these companies is being de-rated on the same unresolved drivers (falling global light-vehicle production, the shift to electric drivetrains, and an unsettled tariff regime), so the gap between CIE and the wider market is sector beta rather than idiosyncratic edge. The one genuinely name-specific relative-value lever is internal, not external: the 65.7% stake in CIE Automotive India is quoted in Mumbai at about 17.5 times earnings while the parent trades at about 8.6 times, so a business worth EUR 944m at market sits inside a company worth EUR 3.07bn. That gap is measurable and specific to CIE.
interrogator_dossier:
# Forensic dossier — CIE Automotive, S.A. (CIE.MC, Bolsa de Madrid)

**Prepared 27 July 2026. Price used throughout: €25.85 (live quote, Bolsa de Madrid, 27 July 2026). Market value about €3.07 billion.**

**A note on sources.** No earnings-call transcript was bundled with this file, and the licensed market-data feed carries no transcript for this listing. What follows is built from the company's own first-half 2026 results release and results presentation of 23–24 July 2026, a published summary of the 24 July 2026 analyst call (Investing.com), the first-quarter release of 12 May 2026, five years of audited financial statements, and live market prices. Where I attribute words to management, they come from that published call summary and the results release rather than from a verbatim transcript I have read end to end, and I say so. I have invented nothing.

---

## 1. Narrative arc

CIE Automotive makes metal and plastic components for carmakers — forged, machined, stamped, cast, aluminium and plastic parts, plus roof systems — from about 15 countries, and sells them to essentially every large vehicle manufacturer. It is a Spanish mid-cap, headquartered in Bilbao, and it owns 65.7% of a separately listed Indian subsidiary, CIE Automotive India.

The story management has told over the past five years has been unusually consistent, which is itself a finding. Three threads run through it without interruption:

**Thread one: "we grow faster than the market, whatever the market does."** This has been the spine of the message since the 2021–2025 strategic plan was launched, and it survived the chip shortage, the energy shock and now a shrinking global vehicle market. In the first half of 2026 the company put a number on it: sales grew 9.3% at constant exchange rates against a weighted global market that fell 1.0%, an outperformance of 10.3 percentage points. On the July call, corporate development director Lorea de Izaga put the thesis in one line: "If the market shrinks a little bit, that doesn't mean that CIE is not going to carry on growing."

**Thread two: "margins are the discipline, not the ambition."** Management has never promised margin expansion in any given year; it promises to *defend* the margin. The decade record supports the framing — the operating cash margin (EBITDA, or earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, divided by sales) went from 16.5% in 2016 to 19.1% in the first half of 2026, and the operating margin from 11.4% to 14.3%. But note carefully what the *current* year says: the first-half 2026 margin of 19.1% compares with 19.0% a year earlier. Flat. The expansion is a decade story that has plateaued.

**Thread three: "cash conversion is the scoreboard."** The company guides to turning 65% of EBITDA into operating cash flow. In the first half of 2026 it turned 71.2% — €275.1 million on €401.1 million of EBITDA. This is the one place where management has systematically set a bar and then cleared it.

**What changed in 2026.** Two things. First, the 2021–2025 plan was completed and declared delivered in full, closing with a record €336 million of net profit for 2025. Second, and more consequentially, the company shifted from a five-year strategic plan to a much shorter "2026–2027 roadmap" — a narrower, two-year horizon with softer commitments (grow above the market by a low-to-mid single-digit margin at constant currencies; hold 2025 profit levels; convert 65% of EBITDA to cash; cumulative operating funds from operations above €1 billion over the period). Shortening the planning horizon in a shrinking end-market is a defensive move, and it is the single clearest tonal shift in the narrative.

**What was quietly added.** Acquisitions came back to the front of the story. CIE bought Aludec, a decorative-components maker with ten plants (eight in Europe, two in North America), completing on 3 March 2026 for an enterprise value of about €200 million and a total acquisition cost of €270.6 million. On the 24 July call, management said several further targets were entering due diligence in August and September and that a completed deal could produce a "significant leap" in the company's scale.

**What was quietly dropped.** Nothing was dropped so much as refused. The board, per the July call, is "very unhappy" with where the shares trade — and then ruled out buying them back at current prices. That is the most revealing sentence of the year, and section 6 returns to it.

---

## 2. Claims versus financials (forensic)

This is where the record-headline story needs taking apart. The company's first-half 2026 release is headed by records — best half in its history, first half-year with EBITDA above €400 million, record net profit. All three statements are true. They are also, on the arithmetic, considerably less impressive than they sound.

| Management claim | The number | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Record first half" — net profit €191.3m, +2.9% year on year | Correct as reported | **True but acquisition-funded.** Aludec contributed €13.5m of net profit in its first four months. Strip it out and first-half profit was about €177.8m against €185.9m a year earlier — a decline of roughly 4.4%. |
| Sales €2,103.8m, +5.2% | Correct | **80% of the growth was bought.** Aludec added €82.7m of the roughly €104m increase. Organic reported growth was about +1.0%. |
| "Grew 9.3% at constant currency versus a market down 1.0% — 10.3 points of outperformance" | Correct as stated | **Overstates the organic edge.** Aludec is worth about 4.1 points of that 9.3%. Organic constant-currency growth was roughly +5.2%, so genuine organic outperformance is about 6 points, not 10. Still very good — but 6, not 10. |
| "Margins virtually unchanged" — EBITDA 19.1%, operating margin 14.3% | Correct (19.0% and about 14.3% a year earlier) | **True, and the honest framing.** Management is not claiming expansion. |
| Cash conversion 71.2% of EBITDA versus a 65% target | €275.1m operating cash flow; free cash flow €193.4m after €85.4m of capital spending | **Delivered, and the cleanest number in the file.** |
| Leverage improving — net financial debt €962.4m, 1.19 times EBITDA versus 1.26 times a year earlier | Correct as the company defines it | **True, and achieved while paying €70.3m to shareholders and €172.7m for acquisitions in the same six months.** Genuinely difficult. |

Three further cross-checks matter.

**The gap between operating profit and net profit is widening.** First-half EBITDA rose 5.8% and operating profit about 5.1%, but net profit only 2.9%. The wedge is interest on the cash used for Aludec (€270.6m of acquisition cost, €172.7m of it paid out in the half) and the share of profit that belongs to minority shareholders, chiefly in India. In 2025 the company paid €110.5 million of interest on about €2.09 billion of gross borrowings. The operating business is doing better than the bottom line shows, and the bottom line is what the market pays for.

**Currency is doing real damage.** Reported sales grew 5.2% while constant-currency sales grew 9.3% — a 4.1-point translation drag, driven by weakness in the Indian rupee and the Brazilian real against the euro. This is not an operating problem and it can reverse: the euro has weakened against the dollar over the past quarter (1.1377 versus a 200-day average near 1.16), which would turn part of that headwind into a tailwind in the second half.

**Two numbers in the screening file are wrong and should not be used.** The screen carries a trailing-twelve-month diluted earnings figure of €5.55 and trailing free cash flow of €739 million. Neither is real. Audited 2025 diluted earnings were €2.82 a share and 2025 free cash flow was €395 million; on a trailing basis through June 2026, earnings per share are about €2.87 and free cash flow roughly €440 million. The screen also flags a "contracting" gross margin of 21.5% — but the same source reports a 38.9% gross margin for 2024 on virtually identical sales, which is a change in how costs were classified, not a seventeen-point collapse in profitability. The EBITDA margin, which is classification-proof, went 19.3% (2024) to 18.9% (2025) to 19.1% (first half 2026). Essentially flat.

**Capital allocation, tested against the record.** This is where the company earns its stripes. Aludec cost about €200 million in enterprise value and contributed €17.3 million of operating profit and €13.5 million of net profit in four months. Annualised — and first-period figures deserve caution, because purchase accounting can flatter them — that is an earnings yield on the purchase price in the mid-teens. Over five years the company has bought back €96 million of stock (2022 and 2025), raised the dividend from €61 million (2021) to €110 million (2025), and still cut net debt. Return on equity has run between 22% and 26% every year since 2022. Return on invested capital has risen from 8.5% (2022) to 9.4% (2025) — improving, but only around the cost of capital for a business of this risk, which is the honest ceiling on how good this franchise is.

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Rating: stable, with a defensive tilt in the planning horizon.**

The language is confident and has stayed confident. The 24 July release quotes chief executive Jesús María Herrera saying the half "confirms that, after several years of consistent execution, we have consolidated a solid industrial model capable of generating profitable growth, industry-leading margins and high levels of cash." On the call itself he was blunter about the company's ability to absorb an acquisition, pay a dividend and hold leverage all at once: "I know of no other companies that can do it in that manner."

Two markers push against reading this as rising confidence:

**The planning horizon shortened.** The company moved from a five-year plan (2021–2025) to a two-year "roadmap" (2026–2027). Firms extend their horizon when they feel good about the road ahead and shorten it when they do not.

**Management talked down its own consensus.** On the 24 July call, management said the Bloomberg consensus for net results was "somewhat optimistic." Companies rarely volunteer that their analysts are too bullish. It is a mark of candour — and it is a warning that the €3.09 per-share consensus for 2026 is above what the company expects to deliver.

The mix of language has also shifted from offence to a balance of offence and defence: the acquisitions and India greenfield investment are the offensive half; "defend the margin," "hold 2025 profit levels," and a two-year horizon are the defensive half. That is appropriate for a supplier facing a global market forecast at 91.1 million light vehicles in 2026 against 93.1 million in 2025, with a second half expected to fall about 3%.

## 4. Guidance credibility

**Reliability: high.**

The evidence:

- The 2021–2025 strategic plan was completed with all targets met and a record €336 million of net profit in the final year. The company does not have a history of missing its own plan.
- The cash-conversion target of 65% of EBITDA was beaten at 71.2% in the first half of 2026. This is the target management repeats most often, and it clears it.
- The 2026 full-year outlook was reaffirmed at the half, with the second half expected to look like the first apart from normal seasonality — a specific, falsifiable statement rather than a hedge.
- Management volunteered that consensus is too optimistic. That is the opposite of sandbagging-into-a-beat: it lowers the bar honestly rather than gaming it.

Two qualifications. First, quarterly delivery against analysts' numbers has been marginally soft: the street's average estimate for 2025 was €2.88 a share and the company delivered €2.82. Second, forward commitments have become vaguer — "low-to-mid single-digit outperformance" and "maintain 2025 profit levels" are looser than a five-year numeric plan. Credible, but committing to less.

## 5. Analyst pressure points

From the 24 July call, the questions clustered on five things, and the pattern of what management answered concretely versus generally is informative.

**Answered with specifics:** India (market share, greenfield expansion, the priority of profitability over volume, an operating margin near 15%); Brazil (sales up 23% against a market up 10%); European share gains and the electrified-vehicle mix reaching 30% of European sales; working-capital efficiency.

**Answered generally — and these are the pressure points:**

- **North American tariffs and the Mexico-to-United States production shift.** North America is 25.7% of sales and the only large region going backwards (sales down 3.4% against a market down about 1%). The tariff architecture is unsettled: the United States' Section 122 authority lapsed by statute on 24 July 2026, the same week CIE reported, and the proposed replacement covering roughly 60 economies at 10% to 12.5% is not final. Management described reallocating production but did not quantify the cost or the capital required. This is the largest unpriced operational question in the file.
- **China.** Sales fell 11.7%, underperforming the local market by more than six points, with production down 5% in the half. Management's answer — that CIE holds about 70% of its Chinese sales with local Chinese manufacturers — describes the position without addressing why the position is shrinking.
- **Raw-material costs from the Iran conflict**, affecting plastics and aluminium. Acknowledged, not quantified. With Brent crude near $89 and the Strait of Hormuz blockaded again since mid-July 2026, this is live rather than hypothetical.
- **Buybacks.** Asked directly, management said the board is very unhappy with the valuation and then declined to buy stock. See section 6.
- **Inorganic versus organic growth.** Management pointed to several targets entering due diligence in August and September and to a possible "significant leap" in scale. No target, no size, no multiple.

What analysts worry about that management is not addressing: nobody on the call appears to have pressed on the fact that, excluding Aludec, first-half profit fell about 4%. That is the question the results deserved.

## 6. Red flags and green flags

**Red flags**

- **The buyback refusal (24 July 2026 call) is the single most important item in this dossier.** A board that says it is "very unhappy" with a share price, sitting on a stock at roughly 8.6 times this year's expected earnings with a free-cash-flow yield above 10%, and which nonetheless will not buy the stock while it is actively hunting acquisitions, is telling shareholders something specific: that it believes third-party assets are better value than its own equity. It may be right — the Aludec economics suggest it often is — but it removes the most direct lever for closing the discount and hands the outcome to deal execution.
- **Excluding the acquisition, first-half profit fell about 4.4% year on year.** The record headline is real; the underlying trend is not improving.
- **North America and China are both shrinking and both underperforming their markets** (down 3.4% and down 11.7% respectively in the half). Together they are 31.3% of sales.
- **An acquisition-built balance sheet.** Goodwill of €1.76 billion at end-2025 sits against €1.45 billion of equity attributable to shareholders. Growth has been bought, repeatedly and so far well, but the balance sheet has no cushion of tangible book value; tangible asset value is barely positive.
- **The margin sits about 1.26 standard deviations above its own historical peak.** A low multiple on peak margins is a different proposition from a low multiple on normal margins, and the end market is contracting.
- **Thin liquidity.** About 80,000 shares traded on 27 July 2026, roughly €2 million. Entry and exit are constrained.
- **No insider buying** (buy ratio 0.00 in the screening data) and a weak institutional-flow score, in a stock the board itself calls undervalued.

**Green flags**

- **Cash conversion beat its own target by six points** (71.2% versus 65%) while the company simultaneously funded an acquisition and raised the dividend, and leverage still fell to 1.19 times EBITDA from 1.26 times.
- **Aludec looks like a good purchase on the first evidence available**: about €200 million of enterprise value for a business annualising well into double-digit millions of operating profit, integrated inside four months.
- **Genuine organic outperformance of roughly six points** against a shrinking global market, sustained across Europe, Brazil and India simultaneously.
- **A dated, escalating shareholder-return commitment**: a 42% dividend payout for 2026 rising to 50% for 2027, with net debt guided below 0.7 times EBITDA by end-2027.
- **A ten-year record that is hard to argue with**: 6% compound sales growth, 8% compound EBITDA, operating margin from 11.4% to 14.3%, through a pandemic, a semiconductor famine and an energy shock.
- **Management told the market its consensus was too high.** That costs them nothing but credibility they clearly value.

## 7. Hidden signals

**The listed Indian subsidiary is the loudest signal in the file, and nobody discusses it.** CIE owns 65.7% of CIE Automotive India, which is separately quoted in Mumbai at about ₹15,677 crore — roughly €1.44 billion at today's euro/rupee rate of 109.09. CIE's stake is therefore worth about €944 million on the open market. The parent's entire market value is €3.07 billion. So a business representing 16.8% of sales and 15.9% of EBITDA accounts for 31% of the parent's market value, and it trades in India at about 17.5 times earnings while the parent trades at roughly 8.6 times. The other four-fifths of CIE — Europe, North America, Brazil, China — is being valued at something close to €2.1 billion, or around seven times its share of earnings. That is a holding-company discount hiding in plain sight, and it is measurable rather than argued.

**"Roadmap" replaced "strategic plan."** Word choice matters when a company has run five-year plans for two decades.

**Guidance moved from absolute numbers to relative ones.** "Grow above the market" is a promise that can be kept while sales fall. It is the correct promise for the environment, and it is a lower bar.

**Management now quantifies the electrified mix** — 30% of European sales — where it previously spoke of being technology-agnostic. That is a defensive disclosure, pre-empting the question of whether the forging business is tied to the internal-combustion engine.

**The absence of a named acquisition target while flagging a possible "significant leap" in scale** is the kind of language that creates expectation without accountability. Given the buyback refusal, the market is being asked to underwrite a deal it cannot see.

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict

**Trajectory: stable.** The balance sheet is strengthening (leverage down, cash conversion beating target, an acquisition funded from cash flow). The profit and loss account is flat (net profit up 2.9%, down about 4% excluding the acquisition, margins unchanged). Both statements are true at once, and the honest label for that combination is stable rather than strengthening.

**The single thing the director must weigh before sizing:** this board will not buy its own shares at 8.6 times earnings, and intends to spend the cash on other people's companies instead, with due diligence running through August and September 2026. Every element of the value case — the discount to the sum of the parts, the free-cash-flow yield, the deleveraging path to 2027 — depends on that capital being deployed at least as well as Aludec was. There is no share-count mechanism working in the shareholder's favour and no dated event that forces the market to re-price. The stock sits within about 3% of its 52-week low the week after record results. That is the market's verdict on the same facts, and it should be taken seriously rather than dismissed.

**Economic moat: narrow.**

The moat is real but modest, and it is of two kinds. The first is a design-in switching cost: once a component is engineered into a vehicle programme, requalifying a different supplier mid-programme is expensive and slow, so revenue on a won platform is sticky for the five-to-seven-year model life. The second is a scale-and-cost advantage built from a deliberately decentralised, multi-technology operating model that buys underperforming plants cheaply and lifts their margins.

The evidence sets the width. Operating margins of 14.3% and EBITDA margins of 19.1% are far above the peer group — Forvia and Valeo, the two large European comparators, run high-single-digit to low-double-digit EBITDA margins and near-zero or negative returns on equity. That gap is the moat, and it is genuine. But return on invested capital of 9.4% is only around the cost of capital for a cyclical supplier with this leverage, and the returns are lifted by acquisition arithmetic (buy cheap, fix, consolidate) as much as by pricing power. A business with real pricing power would not need to buy its growth. Narrow, not wide.

**Moat trend: stable.** The decade shows widening — margins and returns both up meaningfully since 2016. The current year shows a plateau: margins 19.1% against 19.0%, return on invested capital inching from 9.0% to 9.4%. Calling this "widening" on the strength of the ten-year chart would ignore what the last four half-years actually did.

**Secular threat: manageable.** The structural force worth naming is electrification: as vehicles shift from internal-combustion to electric drivetrains, forged and machined powertrain content — crankshafts, connecting rods, gears — disappears. That is a real erosion channel and it touches a meaningful slice of the forging division. Three pieces of evidence keep it from being terminal. Electrified vehicles already account for 30% of European sales, and CIE's revenue kept growing through that shift. Much of the portfolio is powertrain-agnostic — structural, chassis, body, plastic and decorative parts — and aluminium casting gains content on electric platforms (battery housings, electric-motor housings) rather than losing it. And the company has grown sales at 6% and EBITDA at 8% compound over a decade in an end market that has not grown at all. The cheapness here reads as a fear-print on the whole European supplier cohort rather than a shrinking base — but it is a fear-print on peak margins, which is why the margin of safety needs to be larger than usual to be worth taking.

# Forensic dossier — CIE Automotive, S.A. (CIE.MC, Bolsa de Madrid)

**Prepared 27 July 2026. Price used throughout: €25.85 (live quote, Bolsa de Madrid, 27 July 2026). Market value about €3.07 billion.**

**A note on sources.** No earnings-call transcript was bundled with this file, and the licensed market-data feed carries no transcript for this listing. What follows is built from the company's own first-half 2026 results release and results presentation of 23–24 July 2026, a published summary of the 24 July 2026 analyst call (Investing.com), the first-quarter release of 12 May 2026, five years of audited financial statements, and live market prices. Where I attribute words to management, they come from that published call summary and the results release rather than from a verbatim transcript I have read end to end, and I say so. I have invented nothing.

---

## 1. Narrative arc

CIE Automotive makes metal and plastic components for carmakers — forged, machined, stamped, cast, aluminium and plastic parts, plus roof systems — from about 15 countries, and sells them to essentially every large vehicle manufacturer. It is a Spanish mid-cap, headquartered in Bilbao, and it owns 65.7% of a separately listed Indian subsidiary, CIE Automotive India.

The story management has told over the past five years has been unusually consistent, which is itself a finding. Three threads run through it without interruption:

**Thread one: "we grow faster than the market, whatever the market does."** This has been the spine of the message since the 2021–2025 strategic plan was launched, and it survived the chip shortage, the energy shock and now a shrinking global vehicle market. In the first half of 2026 the company put a number on it: sales grew 9.3% at constant exchange rates against a weighted global market that fell 1.0%, an outperformance of 10.3 percentage points. On the July call, corporate development director Lorea de Izaga put the thesis in one line: "If the market shrinks a little bit, that doesn't mean that CIE is not going to carry on growing."

**Thread two: "margins are the discipline, not the ambition."** Management has never promised margin expansion in any given year; it promises to *defend* the margin. The decade record supports the framing — the operating cash margin (EBITDA, or earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, divided by sales) went from 16.5% in 2016 to 19.1% in the first half of 2026, and the operating margin from 11.4% to 14.3%. But note carefully what the *current* year says: the first-half 2026 margin of 19.1% compares with 19.0% a year earlier. Flat. The expansion is a decade story that has plateaued.

**Thread three: "cash conversion is the scoreboard."** The company guides to turning 65% of EBITDA into operating cash flow. In the first half of 2026 it turned 71.2% — €275.1 million on €401.1 million of EBITDA. This is the one place where management has systematically set a bar and then cleared it.

**What changed in 2026.** Two things. First, the 2021–2025 plan was completed and declared delivered in full, closing with a record €336 million of net profit for 2025. Second, and more consequentially, the company shifted from a five-year strategic plan to a much shorter "2026–2027 roadmap" — a narrower, two-year horizon with softer commitments (grow above the market by a low-to-mid single-digit margin at constant currencies; hold 2025 profit levels; convert 65% of EBITDA to cash; cumulative operating funds from operations above €1 billion over the period). Shortening the planning horizon in a shrinking end-market is a defensive move, and it is the single clearest tonal shift in the narrative.

**What was quietly added.** Acquisitions came back to the front of the story. CIE bought Aludec, a decorative-components maker with ten plants (eight in Europe, two in North America), completing on 3 March 2026 for an enterprise value of about €200 million and a total acquisition cost of €270.6 million. On the 24 July call, management said several further targets were entering due diligence in August and September and that a completed deal could produce a "significant leap" in the company's scale.

**What was quietly dropped.** Nothing was dropped so much as refused. The board, per the July call, is "very unhappy" with where the shares trade — and then ruled out buying them back at current prices. That is the most revealing sentence of the year, and section 6 returns to it.

---

## 2. Claims versus financials (forensic)

This is where the record-headline story needs taking apart. The company's first-half 2026 release is headed by records — best half in its history, first half-year with EBITDA above €400 million, record net profit. All three statements are true. They are also, on the arithmetic, considerably less impressive than they sound.

| Management claim | The number | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Record first half" — net profit €191.3m, +2.9% year on year | Correct as reported | **True but acquisition-funded.** Aludec contributed €13.5m of net profit in its first four months. Strip it out and first-half profit was about €177.8m against €185.9m a year earlier — a decline of roughly 4.4%. |
| Sales €2,103.8m, +5.2% | Correct | **80% of the growth was bought.** Aludec added €82.7m of the roughly €104m increase. Organic reported growth was about +1.0%. |
| "Grew 9.3% at constant currency versus a market down 1.0% — 10.3 points of outperformance" | Correct as stated | **Overstates the organic edge.** Aludec is worth about 4.1 points of that 9.3%. Organic constant-currency growth was roughly +5.2%, so genuine organic outperformance is about 6 points, not 10. Still very good — but 6, not 10. |
| "Margins virtually unchanged" — EBITDA 19.1%, operating margin 14.3% | Correct (19.0% and about 14.3% a year earlier) | **True, and the honest framing.** Management is not claiming expansion. |
| Cash conversion 71.2% of EBITDA versus a 65% target | €275.1m operating cash flow; free cash flow €193.4m after €85.4m of capital spending | **Delivered, and the cleanest number in the file.** |
| Leverage improving — net financial debt €962.4m, 1.19 times EBITDA versus 1.26 times a year earlier | Correct as the company defines it | **True, and achieved while paying €70.3m to shareholders and €172.7m for acquisitions in the same six months.** Genuinely difficult. |

Three further cross-checks matter.

**The gap between operating profit and net profit is widening.** First-half EBITDA rose 5.8% and operating profit about 5.1%, but net profit only 2.9%. The wedge is interest on the cash used for Aludec (€270.6m of acquisition cost, €172.7m of it paid out in the half) and the share of profit that belongs to minority shareholders, chiefly in India. In 2025 the company paid €110.5 million of interest on about €2.09 billion of gross borrowings. The operating business is doing better than the bottom line shows, and the bottom line is what the market pays for.

**Currency is doing real damage.** Reported sales grew 5.2% while constant-currency sales grew 9.3% — a 4.1-point translation drag, driven by weakness in the Indian rupee and the Brazilian real against the euro. This is not an operating problem and it can reverse: the euro has weakened against the dollar over the past quarter (1.1377 versus a 200-day average near 1.16), which would turn part of that headwind into a tailwind in the second half.

**Two numbers in the screening file are wrong and should not be used.** The screen carries a trailing-twelve-month diluted earnings figure of €5.55 and trailing free cash flow of €739 million. Neither is real. Audited 2025 diluted earnings were €2.82 a share and 2025 free cash flow was €395 million; on a trailing basis through June 2026, earnings per share are about €2.87 and free cash flow roughly €440 million. The screen also flags a "contracting" gross margin of 21.5% — but the same source reports a 38.9% gross margin for 2024 on virtually identical sales, which is a change in how costs were classified, not a seventeen-point collapse in profitability. The EBITDA margin, which is classification-proof, went 19.3% (2024) to 18.9% (2025) to 19.1% (first half 2026). Essentially flat.

**Capital allocation, tested against the record.** This is where the company earns its stripes. Aludec cost about €200 million in enterprise value and contributed €17.3 million of operating profit and €13.5 million of net profit in four months. Annualised — and first-period figures deserve caution, because purchase accounting can flatter them — that is an earnings yield on the purchase price in the mid-teens. Over five years the company has bought back €96 million of stock (2022 and 2025), raised the dividend from €61 million (2021) to €110 million (2025), and still cut net debt. Return on equity has run between 22% and 26% every year since 2022. Return on invested capital has risen from 8.5% (2022) to 9.4% (2025) — improving, but only around the cost of capital for a business of this risk, which is the honest ceiling on how good this franchise is.

---

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Rating: stable, with a defensive tilt in the planning horizon.**

The language is confident and has stayed confident. The 24 July release quotes chief executive Jesús María Herrera saying the half "confirms that, after several years of consistent execution, we have consolidated a solid industrial model capable of generating profitable growth, industry-leading margins and high levels of cash." On the call itself he was blunter about the company's ability to absorb an acquisition, pay a dividend and hold leverage all at once: "I know of no other companies that can do it in that manner."

Two markers push against reading this as rising confidence:

**The planning horizon shortened.** The company moved from a five-year plan (2021–2025) to a two-year "roadmap" (2026–2027). Firms extend their horizon when they feel good about the road ahead and shorten it when they do not.

**Management talked down its own consensus.** On the 24 July call, management said the Bloomberg consensus for net results was "somewhat optimistic." Companies rarely volunteer that their analysts are too bullish. It is a mark of candour — and it is a warning that the €3.09 per-share consensus for 2026 is above what the company expects to deliver.

The mix of language has also shifted from offence to a balance of offence and defence: the acquisitions and India greenfield investment are the offensive half; "defend the margin," "hold 2025 profit levels," and a two-year horizon are the defensive half. That is appropriate for a supplier facing a global market forecast at 91.1 million light vehicles in 2026 against 93.1 million in 2025, with a second half expected to fall about 3%.

---

## 4. Guidance credibility

**Reliability: high.**

The evidence:

- The 2021–2025 strategic plan was completed with all targets met and a record €336 million of net profit in the final year. The company does not have a history of missing its own plan.
- The cash-conversion target of 65% of EBITDA was beaten at 71.2% in the first half of 2026. This is the target management repeats most often, and it clears it.
- The 2026 full-year outlook was reaffirmed at the half, with the second half expected to look like the first apart from normal seasonality — a specific, falsifiable statement rather than a hedge.
- Management volunteered that consensus is too optimistic. That is the opposite of sandbagging-into-a-beat: it lowers the bar honestly rather than gaming it.

Two qualifications. First, quarterly delivery against analysts' numbers has been marginally soft: the street's average estimate for 2025 was €2.88 a share and the company delivered €2.82. Second, forward commitments have become vaguer — "low-to-mid single-digit outperformance" and "maintain 2025 profit levels" are looser than a five-year numeric plan. Credible, but committing to less.

---

## 5. Analyst pressure points

From the 24 July call, the questions clustered on five things, and the pattern of what management answered concretely versus generally is informative.

**Answered with specifics:** India (market share, greenfield expansion, the priority of profitability over volume, an operating margin near 15%); Brazil (sales up 23% against a market up 10%); European share gains and the electrified-vehicle mix reaching 30% of European sales; working-capital efficiency.

**Answered generally — and these are the pressure points:**

- **North American tariffs and the Mexico-to-United States production shift.** North America is 25.7% of sales and the only large region going backwards (sales down 3.4% against a market down about 1%). The tariff architecture is unsettled: the United States' Section 122 authority lapsed by statute on 24 July 2026, the same week CIE reported, and the proposed replacement covering roughly 60 economies at 10% to 12.5% is not final. Management described reallocating production but did not quantify the cost or the capital required. This is the largest unpriced operational question in the file.
- **China.** Sales fell 11.7%, underperforming the local market by more than six points, with production down 5% in the half. Management's answer — that CIE holds about 70% of its Chinese sales with local Chinese manufacturers — describes the position without addressing why the position is shrinking.
- **Raw-material costs from the Iran conflict**, affecting plastics and aluminium. Acknowledged, not quantified. With Brent crude near $89 and the Strait of Hormuz blockaded again since mid-July 2026, this is live rather than hypothetical.
- **Buybacks.** Asked directly, management said the board is very unhappy with the valuation and then declined to buy stock. See section 6.
- **Inorganic versus organic growth.** Management pointed to several targets entering due diligence in August and September and to a possible "significant leap" in scale. No target, no size, no multiple.

What analysts worry about that management is not addressing: nobody on the call appears to have pressed on the fact that, excluding Aludec, first-half profit fell about 4%. That is the question the results deserved.

---

## 6. Red flags and green flags

**Red flags**

- **The buyback refusal (24 July 2026 call) is the single most important item in this dossier.** A board that says it is "very unhappy" with a share price, sitting on a stock at roughly 8.6 times this year's expected earnings with a free-cash-flow yield above 10%, and which nonetheless will not buy the stock while it is actively hunting acquisitions, is telling shareholders something specific: that it believes third-party assets are better value than its own equity. It may be right — the Aludec economics suggest it often is — but it removes the most direct lever for closing the discount and hands the outcome to deal execution.
- **Excluding the acquisition, first-half profit fell about 4.4% year on year.** The record headline is real; the underlying trend is not improving.
- **North America and China are both shrinking and both underperforming their markets** (down 3.4% and down 11.7% respectively in the half). Together they are 31.3% of sales.
- **An acquisition-built balance sheet.** Goodwill of €1.76 billion at end-2025 sits against €1.45 billion of equity attributable to shareholders. Growth has been bought, repeatedly and so far well, but the balance sheet has no cushion of tangible book value; tangible asset value is barely positive.
- **The margin sits about 1.26 standard deviations above its own historical peak.** A low multiple on peak margins is a different proposition from a low multiple on normal margins, and the end market is contracting.
- **Thin liquidity.** About 80,000 shares traded on 27 July 2026, roughly €2 million. Entry and exit are constrained.
- **No insider buying** (buy ratio 0.00 in the screening data) and a weak institutional-flow score, in a stock the board itself calls undervalued.

**Green flags**

- **Cash conversion beat its own target by six points** (71.2% versus 65%) while the company simultaneously funded an acquisition and raised the dividend, and leverage still fell to 1.19 times EBITDA from 1.26 times.
- **Aludec looks like a good purchase on the first evidence available**: about €200 million of enterprise value for a business annualising well into double-digit millions of operating profit, integrated inside four months.
- **Genuine organic outperformance of roughly six points** against a shrinking global market, sustained across Europe, Brazil and India simultaneously.
- **A dated, escalating shareholder-return commitment**: a 42% dividend payout for 2026 rising to 50% for 2027, with net debt guided below 0.7 times EBITDA by end-2027.
- **A ten-year record that is hard to argue with**: 6% compound sales growth, 8% compound EBITDA, operating margin from 11.4% to 14.3%, through a pandemic, a semiconductor famine and an energy shock.
- **Management told the market its consensus was too high.** That costs them nothing but credibility they clearly value.

---

## 7. Hidden signals

**The listed Indian subsidiary is the loudest signal in the file, and nobody discusses it.** CIE owns 65.7% of CIE Automotive India, which is separately quoted in Mumbai at about ₹15,677 crore — roughly €1.44 billion at today's euro/rupee rate of 109.09. CIE's stake is therefore worth about €944 million on the open market. The parent's entire market value is €3.07 billion. So a business representing 16.8% of sales and 15.9% of EBITDA accounts for 31% of the parent's market value, and it trades in India at about 17.5 times earnings while the parent trades at roughly 8.6 times. The other four-fifths of CIE — Europe, North America, Brazil, China — is being valued at something close to €2.1 billion, or around seven times its share of earnings. That is a holding-company discount hiding in plain sight, and it is measurable rather than argued.

**"Roadmap" replaced "strategic plan."** Word choice matters when a company has run five-year plans for two decades.

**Guidance moved from absolute numbers to relative ones.** "Grow above the market" is a promise that can be kept while sales fall. It is the correct promise for the environment, and it is a lower bar.

**Management now quantifies the electrified mix** — 30% of European sales — where it previously spoke of being technology-agnostic. That is a defensive disclosure, pre-empting the question of whether the forging business is tied to the internal-combustion engine.

**The absence of a named acquisition target while flagging a possible "significant leap" in scale** is the kind of language that creates expectation without accountability. Given the buyback refusal, the market is being asked to underwrite a deal it cannot see.

---

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict

**Trajectory: stable.** The balance sheet is strengthening (leverage down, cash conversion beating target, an acquisition funded from cash flow). The profit and loss account is flat (net profit up 2.9%, down about 4% excluding the acquisition, margins unchanged). Both statements are true at once, and the honest label for that combination is stable rather than strengthening.

**The single thing the director must weigh before sizing:** this board will not buy its own shares at 8.6 times earnings, and intends to spend the cash on other people's companies instead, with due diligence running through August and September 2026. Every element of the value case — the discount to the sum of the parts, the free-cash-flow yield, the deleveraging path to 2027 — depends on that capital being deployed at least as well as Aludec was. There is no share-count mechanism working in the shareholder's favour and no dated event that forces the market to re-price. The stock sits within about 3% of its 52-week low the week after record results. That is the market's verdict on the same facts, and it should be taken seriously rather than dismissed.

**Economic moat: narrow.**

The moat is real but modest, and it is of two kinds. The first is a design-in switching cost: once a component is engineered into a vehicle programme, requalifying a different supplier mid-programme is expensive and slow, so revenue on a won platform is sticky for the five-to-seven-year model life. The second is a scale-and-cost advantage built from a deliberately decentralised, multi-technology operating model that buys underperforming plants cheaply and lifts their margins.

The evidence sets the width. Operating margins of 14.3% and EBITDA margins of 19.1% are far above the peer group — Forvia and Valeo, the two large European comparators, run high-single-digit to low-double-digit EBITDA margins and near-zero or negative returns on equity. That gap is the moat, and it is genuine. But return on invested capital of 9.4% is only around the cost of capital for a cyclical supplier with this leverage, and the returns are lifted by acquisition arithmetic (buy cheap, fix, consolidate) as much as by pricing power. A business with real pricing power would not need to buy its growth. Narrow, not wide.

**Moat trend: stable.** The decade shows widening — margins and returns both up meaningfully since 2016. The current year shows a plateau: margins 19.1% against 19.0%, return on invested capital inching from 9.0% to 9.4%. Calling this "widening" on the strength of the ten-year chart would ignore what the last four half-years actually did.

**Secular threat: manageable.** The structural force worth naming is electrification: as vehicles shift from internal-combustion to electric drivetrains, forged and machined powertrain content — crankshafts, connecting rods, gears — disappears. That is a real erosion channel and it touches a meaningful slice of the forging division. Three pieces of evidence keep it from being terminal. Electrified vehicles already account for 30% of European sales, and CIE's revenue kept growing through that shift. Much of the portfolio is powertrain-agnostic — structural, chassis, body, plastic and decorative parts — and aluminium casting gains content on electric platforms (battery housings, electric-motor housings) rather than losing it. And the company has grown sales at 6% and EBITDA at 8% compound over a decade in an end market that has not grown at all. The cheapness here reads as a fear-print on the whole European supplier cohort rather than a shrinking base — but it is a fear-print on peak margins, which is why the margin of safety needs to be larger than usual to be worth taking.

CREDIBILITY_SCORE: 4 | TRAJECTORY: STABLE | MOAT: NARROW | MOAT_TREND: STABLE | SECULAR_THREAT: manageable
